## The question

Citing a retracted paper as though it stands is a known failure of the literature, and
meta-research is the field that documents it. Retracted randomized trials have been shown to
go on being cited uncorrected in systematic reviews and clinical guidelines (PMID 35779825),
and clinical practice guidelines for low back pain have been shown to cite retracted and
predatory work (PMID 40156953).

Nobody has turned that instrument on meta-research itself. If a field that studies citation of
retracted work does it at the same rate as everyone else, that is a finding about how far
knowing a problem gets you toward avoiding it.

## Hypothesis

Meta-research articles cite retracted work at a lower rate than a matched comparison of
articles published in the same journals and years.

The direction is stated because the alternative is the interesting one. A field with domain
expertise in this exact failure, finding no advantage from that expertise, says something the
descriptive literature does not.

**What would falsify it.** A rate ratio at or above 1 against the matched comparison. Given the
low base rate of citing retracted work, the study is powered by the number of references, not
the number of articles, and the power calculation is done before the run and reported whatever
it says.

## Unit of analysis

One reference. The 1088 corpus records with PMC full text yield an estimated 60000 to 90000
references, of which roughly 62 percent carry a DOI in the JATS markup, measured on a pilot of
three articles. References without a DOI are not matchable and are excluded; the exclusion rate
is reported per article, since an article whose references are mostly unmatchable contributes
little and a systematic difference in DOI coverage between the corpus and the comparison would
be a confounder in its own right.

## Comparison group

Articles from the same journals and the same publication years that are not in the corpus,
sampled to match the corpus distribution of journal and year, and restricted to those with PMC
full text so that reference extraction is identical for both arms. Matching on journal is not
optional: the corpus is concentrated in a small number of methods journals whose reference
practices are not those of the literature at large.

## Measurement

Retraction Watch is retrieved as an open CSV through Crossref Labs; it carries 72577 records
with `OriginalPaperDOI`, `RetractionDate` and `Reason`. A cited DOI counts as a citation of
retracted work when it appears in that column.

The critical refinement, and the reason a naive version of this study would be wrong: a
reference is only a failure if the retraction preceded the citing article. A paper published
before its source was retracted could not have known. Every match is therefore classified:

| class | meaning |
|---|---|
| post-retraction citation | retraction date precedes the citing article's publication date |
| pre-retraction citation | the citing article came first |
| discussed as retracted | the citing article is about retraction and cites the paper as an example |

The third class is not a small correction here; it is the dominant confounder. Meta-research
about retraction cites retracted papers on purpose, and a study that counted those as failures
would produce exactly the opposite of the truth. Classification uses the `retract` topic label
and the citation context extracted from the surrounding sentence in the JATS body, and every
article carrying the `retract` label is additionally reported separately so the primary estimate
can be read with and without them.

## Analysis

In R. The outcome is a count of post-retraction citations per article with the article's total
matchable references as the offset.

```r
glm.nb(n_post_retraction ~ arm + year_c + offset(log(n_matchable_refs)),
       data = d)
```

Negative binomial rather than Poisson because reference counts of this kind are overdispersed,
with the dispersion parameter reported rather than assumed. A sensitivity analysis excludes
every article carrying the `retract` label from both arms.

## What it costs

1088 PMC full-text fetches, shared with P01 and served from the same cache. One 72577-row CSV.
The comparison arm needs its own PubMed query and PMC fetch, of comparable size. No paid
service.

## Known threats to the result

- **62 percent DOI coverage in reference lists.** If coverage differs between arms the offset is
  biased. Measured and reported per arm before the model is fitted.
- **Retraction Watch is not complete and its dates are not always the publisher's.** A missing
  retraction biases both arms toward the null equally; a systematically late date misclassifies
  post-retraction citations as pre-retraction, again in both arms.
- **The matched comparison is matched on journal and year and nothing else.** Article type,
  length and reference count differ, and the offset handles only the last.
